catalog_quote: Stress is not marked by either Radcliffe-Brown or Man. In none of the languages of the Great Andamanese family (including PGA) is it phonemically relevant. Non-phonemic stress, in all the languages, falls on the initial syllable of the root, at least ordinarily. ... Together with the extinct Akakede language [akx], once spoken on the northern half of Middle Andaman and on Interview Island (Portman 1899: 21), North Andamanese forms one of the three (well-defined) subgroups of the Great Andamanese language family

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim in the held excerpt, the full local text, and the publisher PDF downloaded now (saved with MANIFEST; The deciding work is a 2021 reference grammar, but of a sister language; its stress sentence is a one-line, unsourced family-wide generalisation hedged 'at least ordinarily', and no Akakede data bear on it (Portman 1887, the sole primary source, marks no stress). That makes the record second-hand, hence 'thin', but nothing better exists for an extinct language with 19th-century wordlist attestation only, and nothing seen contradicts root-initial non-phonemic stress (Temple 1903 and Yadav 1985 PGA agree on a first-syllable/root anchor; Blevins 2009's 'not predictable' remark concerns Man's Aka-Bea marks, a different branch). set by morphology (root-initial in a prefixing family) is a fair reading of the quoted sent
